passage:
The demo was due at nine the next morning, and Rehana had four hours. Harish, her old college friend, leaned over. “Just send it to our batch group for feedback. They'll get it fast.”

She almost said yes. Then she noticed the word “our.” Everyone in that group thought like her, which was exactly why it felt easy. Instead she walked to Meera from the accounts team, who had never used the tool. Meera frowned at page two and asked, “Why would I trust this number?” Rehana fixed the label in ten minutes.

At the pantry, someone laughed about how the accounts team talks. Rehana set down her cup. “They stayed until two to close our numbers. Let's not.” Nobody answered, and Harish quietly refilled her tea.

qa.q: Why did Harish suggest sending the demo to the batch group?
qa.a: Harish thought the batch group would understand the demo fast.

qa.q: What did Rehana notice in the word “our” that made her stop?
qa.a: Rehana realised that everyone in that group thought like her, which was why it felt easy, and the ease made her doubt it.

qa.q: Which choice helped improve the demo, and how?
qa.a: Rehana asked Meera, who had never used the tool, and Meera's question about the number led to a quick fix of the label.

qa.q: How might Meera have felt when Rehana came to the accounts desk and later defended the team?
qa.a: Meera would probably feel respected, since Rehana sought Meera's honest view and stood up when the team was laughed at.

grounding: A mature adult checks a comfortable assumption, seeks a different view under time pressure and speaks up when a team is mocked, while staying friends with their college group.

passage:
At the colony's monthly meeting, Dhruv had already decided which way Vidya from the far block would vote. She always objected, he thought. Then he caught himself and asked her outright, “What worries you about the parking plan?” Vidya blinked. “The lane behind B block floods. Nobody has asked us.” It was a fair point he had missed.

Later, three men near the tea table joked about the security guards, mimicking how they speak. Someone laughed. Dhruv put his cup down. “They've watched over our children's cycles for years. Could we not?” One man shrugged, another looked at his shoes, and the laughing stopped.

Dhruv still walked home with his own block friends, chatting as usual. He just no longer needed them to be the only ones who mattered.

qa.q: What did Vidya say worries her about the parking plan?
qa.a: Vidya said the lane behind B block floods and nobody has asked the far block.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv ask Vidya outright about the parking plan?
qa.a: Dhruv felt uneasy on catching himself assuming Vidya would object, and was curious to hear Vidya's real reasons instead of guessing.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do when the joking about the guards began, and what happened next?
qa.a: Dhruv put his cup down and asked them to stop, mentioning the guards' years of watching over the children's cycles, and the laughing stopped.

qa.q: How might one of the guards feel if they had overheard the meeting that evening?
qa.a: They might feel relieved and quietly respected that someone in the group spoke up on their behalf, though the mocking would still sting.

grounding: A mature adult checks assumptions, asks a resident from another block for a view and speaks up when guards are mocked, while staying close to their own friends.

passage:
“These new people in the society,” said Rashmi, laughing at the dinner table. “So loud. Village types. They hang clothes on the balcony like it's a mela.”
Others laughed. Gurleen put down her fork.
“Rashmi, you know the Yadavs on the fourth floor?”
“Sort of.”
“Their daughter helped my mother carry groceries when the lift broke. Twice.”
“Okay, but in general—”
“I'd rather not say ‘in general’ about people I haven't met,” Gurleen said, smiling. “You're my oldest friend. I'm not going anywhere. I just don't want us laughing at them.”
Rashmi rolled her eyes, but then grinned. “Fine. Pass the dal, Mother Teresa.”

qa.q: Who helped Gurleen's mother carry groceries?
qa.a: The Yadavs' daughter helped her, twice.

qa.q: How did Gurleen seem to feel when she put down her fork?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable with the mocking but calm and steady, ready to speak up kindly.

qa.q: What makes Gurleen's way of speaking up effective?
qa.a: She gives a real example, refuses to judge people she hasn't met, and reassures Rashmi of their friendship, so it isn't an attack.

qa.q: How might Rashmi feel after being challenged?
qa.a: Rashmi seems a little annoyed but not hurt, joking back because Gurleen made clear their friendship was safe.

grounding: Shows a young woman speaking up when her friends mock a group, staying loyal to them without needing others to be lesser.

passage:
I'm Tenzin, and two years ago I made a decision that sounds small. I decided to eat lunch with a different group once a week.
At the office, my people were the other northeast folks, and I loved them. But I realised I only knew what we thought. So I joined the accountants, the drivers, the interns.
Once, back at my usual table, Bhupen joked that all the drivers are drunk by evening. The table laughed. I said, “Actually, I had lunch with them Tuesday. Raju drives his daughter to college after his shift. No drinking.” Bhupen shrugged, “Just a joke, yaar.” I said, “I know. Still.”
I'm still at that table most days. I still love them. I just know more people now.

qa.q: Who drives his daughter to college after his shift?
qa.a: Raju does.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when the table laughed at the joke?
qa.a: Tenzin felt uncomfortable but steady, confident enough to share a real example without getting angry.

qa.q: Why is Tenzin's weekly lunch habit a wise choice?
qa.a: It deliberately exposes Tenzin to different views, so Tenzin can question jokes about groups with real knowledge.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Tenzin's comment?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel slightly caught out, shrugging it off as a joke, but has now heard a real example that questions it.

grounding: A young adult describes deliberately seeking out other groups and speaking up when one is mocked, while staying loyal to their own friends.

passage:
Supervisor's note, customer service team, Friday.
Our new hire, Saurabh, joined from a village near Sagar. At lunch this week, a few team members mimicked his Hindi and called him “gaon ka hero.” He laughed along, but ate faster and left early.
Today Sonali, who has been with us two years, said at the table, quite gently, “Guys, can we drop that? Saurabh has handled more calls than any of us this week.” Then she moved her tray and sat next to him. She is still very much part of the old group. Nobody seemed angry with her.
I thanked Sonali privately. I will also remind the team about respectful conduct at Monday's meeting, without naming anyone.

qa.q: What did some team members call Saurabh?
qa.a: They called him "gaon ka hero".

qa.q: How did Saurabh seem to feel during the mimicking?
qa.a: He seemed embarrassed and uncomfortable, laughing along but eating faster and leaving early.

qa.q: What did Sonali do that made a difference?
qa.a: She asked the group gently to stop, gave a fact about Saurabh's work, and sat with him, while staying part of the old group.

qa.q: How might the team members who mimicked feel after Sonali spoke?
qa.a: They might feel a little embarrassed but not attacked, since she was kind and still one of them.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young worker speaking up when a new colleague is mocked, while staying loyal to her own group.

passage:
Thursday night.
Dinner at Harman's with the college gang. Loved it, as always: same jokes, same arguments about cricket.
Then Harman started mimicking "those people from the old city" and their accent. Everyone laughed. I laughed at the first line too, out of habit. Then I thought of Wasim from my team, who grew up there, who stayed back two nights last month to fix my broken report.
I said, "Yaar, Wasim talks like that, and he's the sharpest person in our office. Leave it." It came out calmer than I felt. Harman rolled his eyes. "Relax, Baljeet." Then the talk drifted back to cricket. Nobody stayed annoyed for long.
Driving home, I kept wondering what else I've laughed at without noticing. I've asked Wasim to lunch on Saturday. I want to actually hear about his neighbourhood instead of guessing.
I still love that lot. I just don't need anyone to be lesser for us to be close.

qa.q: How many nights did Wasim stay back to fix the report?
qa.a: Two nights last month.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when speaking up at dinner?
qa.a: Baljeet felt more upset inside than it sounded, "calmer than I felt", but steady and still fond of the group.

qa.q: Why is asking Wasim to lunch a good next step for Baljeet?
qa.a: It replaces guesses about the old city with a real person's view, which is how Baljeet can check other assumptions too.

qa.q: How might Harman see Baljeet's comment?
qa.a: Harman seems mildly irritated, rolling his eyes, but not deeply offended, since the evening goes on as usual.

grounding: Shows a young adult checking a habit of laughing along, speaking up calmly when a group is mocked, and seeking other views while staying loyal to friends.
